title: Reasoning in Reference Games: Individual- vs. Population-Level Probabilistic Modeling

source.title: Reasoning in Reference Games: Individual- vs. Population-Level Probabilistic Modeling

studies.title: Experiment 1: comprehension in reference games
studies.description: Mechanical Turk participants choose the intended referent among three objects after seeing a pictorial one-feature message; simple and complex ad hoc Quantity implicature trials plus fillers.

studies.title: Experiment 2: production in reference games
studies.description: Mechanical Turk participants choose one of four pictorial messages to describe a highlighted object in the same games.

studies.title: Individual-level hierarchical modelling and Bayesian model comparison
studies.description: Latent reasoning-type model fitted to the individual choice counts of Experiments 1 and 2, with homogeneous (Gricean) versus heterogeneous population comparison. Analysis scope, not an experiment.

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Two online behavioural experiments (reference-game comprehension and production) analysed with a hierarchical Bayesian latent-type model; a third experiment eliciting salience priors is reported only in a supplement (S4 Text).

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: The paper asks whether speakers and listeners are Gricean individually or only on average, using reference games that need ad hoc Quantity implicatures of varying complexity. A heterogeneous mix of reasoning types predicts the data better than a homogeneous Gricean population, especially for comprehension.

fields.label: Research question
fields.value: Are listeners and speakers Gricean at the individual level or only at the population level?

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: Probabilistic pragmatics models are usually assessed on population-level data obtained by averaging over participants, which implicitly assumes a homogeneous population.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: Rational Speech Act (Gricean S1 speaker, R2 listener) versus iterated best response types S0, S1, S2 and R0, R1, R2 with increasing Theory-of-Mind depth.

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The population of participants is a heterogeneous mix of pragmatic reasoning types (null hypothesis: all participants are Gricean S1 speakers and R2 listeners); the heterogeneous model is expected to predict individual-level data better than the homogeneous model.

fields.label: Scope
fields.value: Production and comprehension in the monsters-and-robots reference games.

fields.label: Validity statements
fields.value: Results are contingent on the particular task, the data and the specific modelling choices; reference-game data do not necessarily generalise to other areas of language use.

fields.label: Modelling limitations
fields.value: Population-level lambda and epsilon are shared across reasoning types and participants; reasoning type is assumed constant over the experiment, which the authors call generally dubious.

fields.label: Replications the paper reports
fields.value: Experiment 1 is described as a replication of Experiment 1 of reference [9]; Experiment 2 as a replication of Experiment 2 of [9], with caveats (target choices slightly above chance in the complex condition, below ceiling in the simple condition).

fields.label: Materials
fields.value: Links to all experiments are given in S3 Text and the derivations in S1, S2, S4 and S5 Text; these supplements are not in paper.pdf.

fields.label: Aim
fields.value: Infer each participant's likely reasoning type (S0/S1/S2 for production, R0/R1/R2 for comprehension) and the population distribution over types, and decide whether the homogeneous Gricean model suffices.

fields.value: Binomial likelihood with probabilities determined by the participant's type, population error rate epsilon and rationality lambda; types drawn from a categorical population distribution with a Dirichlet(1,1,1) prior; Gamma priors on epsilon and lambda; JAGS, 10000 samples after 10000 burn-in, two chains, thinning 2.

fields.label: Criterion
fields.value: Bayes factors greater than 3 count as sufficiently strong evidence for a model.

fields.label: Computation details
fields.value: Details of the approximation are in S5 Text, which is not in the paper.

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Result kind
fields.value: reported

fields.label: Test
fields.value: With tolerance 0.05: production BF(hom/het) about 3.955 (favours the near-homogeneous model); comprehension about 2.8e-11 (strongly favours heterogeneous). With tolerance 0.01 for production the BF is 0.004 (about 250 for heterogeneous).

fields.label: Answer

fields.label: Support

evidence.quote: Here we investigate potential individual differences in Theory-of-Mind related depth of pragmatic reasoning in so-called reference games that require drawing ad hoc Quantity implicatures of varying complexity.
We show by Bayesian model comparison that a model that assumes a heterogenous population is a better predictor of our data, especially for comprehension.

model predictions are usually assessed based on population-level data from suitable experimental tasks. That is, the data to be explained by a given model are obtained by averaging over the answers of all participants.

We formulate models of different complexity: one that assumes a homogeneous population of Gricean speakers and listeners, and one that assumes a heterogeneous population with varying proportions of pragmatic reasoning types inspired by game-theoretic approaches.
There are three referents and four possible messages, which are assumed to be common ground between speaker and listener.
The speaker ’s task is to describe the trigger referent (marked by an asterisk) with one of the message options from set
Level-( n + 1) language users choose optimal signals or interpretations based on the belief that the other player is a level- n player.
Table 1 summarizes the reasoning types that we consider here, their level of Theory-of-Mind reasoning and the choices these idealized types would make in the simple and complex games from Fig 1.
We then compare a homogeneous “null-model” that contains only the Gricean types to a “saturated model” that contains all of the archetypes from Table 1.
Since the simpler model is a special case of the complex model, the latter will be able to accommodate every data observation at least as well as the former.

Experiment 1 tests the comprehension of referential expressions in reference games like the ones introduced in Fig 1. Experiment 2 tests the production of referential expressions in the same games. Experiment 3 (see S4 Text) elicits salience priors over objects required for modeling the R2 listener.
Conclusions based on data from reference games do not necessarily generalize to other areas of language use

60 participants were recruited via Amazon ’s Web Service Mechanical Turk. Participants’ IP address was limited to US addresses only. Only participants with a past work approval rate of at least 95% were accepted.
All participants gave written consent and received $1.00 for their participation (hourly rate of $10.00) according to the policies set forth by the Stanford University research subjects review board.

Participants engaged in a referential comprehension task. On each trial they saw three objects on a display. Each object differed systematically along two dimensions: its ontological kind (robot, green monster, purple monster) and accessory (scarf, blue hat, red hat).

In addition to these three objects, participants saw a pictorial message that they were told was sent to them by a previous participant whose goal was to get them to pick out one of these three objects.

They were told that the previous participant was allowed to send a message expressing only one feature of a given object, and that the messages the participant could send were furthermore restricted to monsters and hats
The four expressible features were visible to participants at the bottom of the display on every trial

Participants initially completed four speaker trials. They saw three objects, one of which was highlighted with a yellow rectangle. Participants were asked to click on one of four pictorial messages to send to another Mechanical Turk worker to get them to pick out the highlighted object.
The four speaker trials contained three unambiguous and one ambiguous trial which could function as fillers in the main experiment.
Participants saw 66 experimental trials, which were composed of 24 critical and 42 filler trials. Of the 24 critical trials, 12 constituted a simple implicature situation and 12 a complex one
Stimuli were created by randomly sampling a message and then generating a grid of three objects —a target, a competitor, and a distractor — following different constraints in different conditions.
On simple implicature trials, the target was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with the inexpressible feature along the other feature dimension.
The competitor was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with a randomly sampled expressible feature along the other feature dimension.
The distractor was generated by combining two features that were randomly sampled from the set of features that did not contain those features already present in target and competitor.
On complex implicature trials, the target was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with an expressible feature along the other feature dimension.
The competitor was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with the remaining expressible feature along the other feature dimension.
The distractor was generated by combining the target feature that was not denoted by the sampled message (red hat) with the inexpressible feature along the other feature dimension (robot).

Of the 42 filler trials, 24 used the displays from the implicature conditions but the target was a) the competitor from the simple condition (six trials), b) the distractor from the simple condition (six trials), or c) the competitor from the complex condition (12 trials), as identified unambiguously by the trigger message.

On the other 18 filler trials, the target was either entirely unambiguous or entirely ambiguous given the message. That is, there was either only one object with the feature denoted by the trigger message, or there were two identical objects that were equally viable target candidates.
Trial order as well as target, competitor, and distractor order were randomized.
Those 15% of participants with the highest error rate (distractor responses) on trials that were not ambiguous were excluded from the analysis.
The data from the 51 remaining participants entered the analysis.

participants were close to ceiling in choosing the target on unambiguous filler trials (99% target choices vs..04% competitor choices) but at chance on ambiguous ones (46% target choices vs. 51% competitor choices).

On simple implicature trials, participants chose the target 77% of the time and the competitor 23% of the time. On complex implicature trials, the target was chosen less often (57% target choices vs. 42% competitor choices).

A logistic mixed-effects regression was conducted to assess whether the observed differences in target choices between the ambiguous and complex, and the complex and simple condition, were significantly different.
Trials on which the distractor was selected were excluded to allow for a binary outcome variable (target vs. competitor choice). This led to an exclusion of 1% of the data.

This experiment constitutes a replication of Experiment 1 of [ 9].

60 participants were recruited via Amazon ’s Web Service Mechanical Turk. Participants’ IP address was limited to US addresses only. Only participants with a past work approval rate of at least 95% were accepted.
The procedure was identical to that on speaker trials in Experiment 1.
Each participant saw 66 experimental trials. The distribution of trial types was the same as in Experiment 1: 24 critical trials (12 simple, 12 complex, see Fig 1) and 42 filler trials.

Each of the four messages received a trial by trial status as target, competitor, distractor 1, or distractor 2. Stimuli were created by randomly sampling a message and then generating a grid of three objects following different constraints in different conditions. The sampled message was the target.

On simple implicature trials, the trigger object was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with an expressible feature along the other feature dimension. The message denoting this other feature was the competitor message.
A second object was generated by combining the feature denoted by the competitor message with the inexpressible feature along the other feature dimension.
A third object was generated by combining the two remaining expressible features. The messages denoting these features were randomly deemed distractor 1 or distractor 2.
On complex implicature trials, the trigger object was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with an expressible feature along the other feature dimension.

A third object was generated by combining the feature denoted by the sampled message with the remaining expressible feature along the other feature dimension. In our example: a green monster with a blue hat.

Of the 42 filler trials, 24 used the displays from the implicature conditions but the highlighted trigger object was a) the competitor from the simple condition (six trials), b) the distractor from the simple condition (six trials), or c) the distractor from the complex condition (12 trials).

On the remaining 18 filler trials, the target message to refer to the highlighted object was either entirely unambiguous (because the other feature was one of the inexpressible robot or scarf features) or entirely ambiguous (because no other object in the display had the trigger object features but each trigger object feature was an equally good message choice).
Trial order, position of the trigger object in the grid, and order of target, competitor, and distractor messages were randomized.
Again, the 15% of participants with the highest error rate on trials that were not ambiguous were excluded.
The data from 50 remaining participants entered the analysis.

participants were close to ceiling in choosing the target on unambiguous filler trials (96% target choices vs. 1% competitor choices) but at chance on ambiguous ones (48% target choices vs. 48% competitor choices).

On simple implicature trials, participants chose the target 82% of the time and the competitor 16% of the time. On complex implicature trials, the target was chosen less often (53% target choices vs. 45% competitor choices).

The mixed effects logistic regression analysis was conducted as in Experiment 1 and predicted target over competitor message choices. The only differences were that a) the random effects structure consisted only of random by-participant intercepts
participants made more target choices in simple than in complex implicature situations (β = 1.63, SE = .13, p <.0001).
participants only made marginally more target choices in complex implicature situations than on ambiguous filler trials (β = .2, SE = .11, p <.08)
participants became overall slightly less likely to choose targets as the experiment progressed (β = -.01, SE = .003, p <.05).

The main goal of this section is to assess whether it is plausible to maintain the “null hypothesis” that all participants in our experiments can be construed as Gricean, i.e., as S1 and R2 respectively.
Resulting predictions are well-aligned with the observations, as shown in Fig 4 (correlation r = 0.997, p < 0.0001).
we take a hierarchical modeling approach [ 63] in which the simpler Gricean model is nested under the more complex heterogeneous type model.

the data that we would like to explain are counts dXijk, one set for production (X = S) and one for comprehension ( X = R), giving the number of choices across the whole experiment of participant i for game j (simple, complex, unambiguous, ambiguous) that fell into category k
We assume that each participant i has a ﬁxed type τi 2 {0, 1, 2} that is constant across the experiment.
The likelihood of each dXijk is then given by the binomial distribution
We assume largely uninformative prior probabilities for parameter values

issues.title: Supplementary texts S1-S5 and Experiment 3 are not available
issues.reason: Experiment 3 (salience priors), the derivation of idealised predictions (S1), type definitions (S2), experiment links (S3) and Bayes factor computation (S5) are in supplements that are not part of paper.pdf.
issues.impact: Experiment 3 is not modelled as a study; exact printed instructions, stimulus images and the salience priors needed for the R2 listener rule cannot be reproduced from the paper alone.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply S1-S5 Text or the experiment materials in sources/ to extend the program.

issues.title: exp1: sample characteristics and completion counts not reported
issues.reason: The paper gives no age, gender or the number who completed versus started.
issues.impact: AI participants cannot be matched to the human sample demographically; no persona is simulated.
issues.suggestedAction: Treat participants as unconditioned AI participants or supply demographics.

issues.title: exp1: number completed not stated
issues.reason: Only the recruited (60) and analysed counts are reported.
issues.impact: Randomised, retained and analysed sizes cannot be fully distinguished.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the completion count.

issues.title: exp1: blinding not reported
issues.reason: The paper does not state blinding.
issues.impact: No effect on the replay; participants are AI.
issues.suggestedAction: None needed unless the researcher wants a statement.

issues.title: exp1: printed instructions and stimuli not in the paper
issues.reason: The paper paraphrases what participants were told but prints no instruction text, screen or picture.
issues.impact: The replay prompts use a paraphrase of the reported instructions and text descriptions of objects and messages; this is a replay adaptation, not the original material.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the original instruction text and stimulus pictures in sources/ to make them verbatim.

issues.title: exp1: stimuli are pictures
issues.reason: The original stimuli are pictures (Fig 1) which text-only AI participants cannot see.
issues.impact: Objects and messages are rendered as text such as 'a green monster with a red hat'.
issues.suggestedAction: Accept the text rendering or provide image-capable participants.

issues.title: exp1: filler displays under-specified
issues.reason: The 18 baseline fillers are described only as unambiguous or ambiguous; the split between the two kinds, the number of distinct displays and scoring details are not stated.
issues.impact: The replay chooses an even split (9 and 9) and the construction rules documented in task/task.json.
issues.suggestedAction: Supply the split and the filler construction or confirm the assumption.

issues.title: exp1: feedback not reported
issues.reason: The paper does not say whether participants received feedback on their choices.
issues.impact: The replay gives no feedback; if feedback existed, learning might differ.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm that no feedback was given.

issues.title: exp1: counterpart of the participant not specified
issues.reason: It is not stated whether the messages (comprehension) or the addressee (production) were real participants or scripted.
issues.impact: In the replay the message is the generated trigger message (a scripted stimulus) and no real addressee exists; this follows the stimulus description and is the only runnable reading.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm that messages were generated from the design, not taken from earlier participants.

issues.title: exp1: Helmert contrast scaling not stated
issues.reason: The contrast weights are not printed, so coefficients are only comparable with the paper up to the coding.
issues.impact: The evaluator uses standard Helmert weights and fixed-effects logistic regression and flags the difference to the paper's mixed-effects model.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm weights or run glmer externally.
